# chrono - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/chrono/0.4.45/chrono/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#chrono-date-and-time-for-rust)Chrono: Date and Time for Rust

Chrono aims to provide all functionality needed to do correct operations on dates and times in
the [proleptic Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proleptic_Gregorian_calendar):

- The `DateTime`
- Operations that may produce an invalid or ambiguous date and time return `Option`or`MappedLocalTime`
- Configurable parsing and formatting with a `strftime`inspired date and time formatting syntax.
- The `Local`
- Types and operations are implemented to be reasonably efficient.

Timezone data is not shipped with chrono by default to limit binary sizes. Use the companion
crate [Chrono-TZ](https://crates.io/crates/chrono-tz) or [ tzfile](https://crates.io/crates/tzfile) for full timezone support.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Chrono supports various runtime environments and operating systems, and has several features that may be enabled or disabled.

Default features:

- `alloc`: Enable features that depend on allocation (primarily string formatting).
- `std`: Enables functionality that depends on the standard library. This is a superset of- `alloc`and adds interoperation with standard library types and traits.
- `clock`: Enables reading the local timezone (- `Local`). This is a superset of- `now`.
- `now`: Enables reading the system time (- `now`).
- `wasmbind`: Interface with the JS Date API for the- `wasm32`target.

Optional features:

- `serde`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde).
- `rkyv`: Deprecated, use the- `rkyv-*`features.
- `rkyv-16`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 16-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-32`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 32-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-64`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 64-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-validation`: Enable rkyv validation support using- `bytecheck`.
- `arbitrary`: Construct arbitrary instances of a type with the Arbitrary crate.
- `unstable-locales`: Enable localization. This adds various methods with a- `_localized`suffix. The implementation and API may change or even be removed in a patch release. Feedback welcome.
- `oldtime`: This feature no longer has any effect; it used to offer compatibility with the- `time`0.1 crate.

Note: The `rkyv{,-16,-32,-64}` features are mutually exclusive.

See the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#choosing-features) for examples of specifying features.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

[§](https://docs.rs#time-delta--duration)Time delta / Duration

Chrono has a [ TimeDelta](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html) type to represent the magnitude of a time span. This is an “accurate”
duration represented as seconds and nanoseconds, and does not represent “nominal” components
such as days or months.

The [ TimeDelta](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html) type was previously named

`Duration` (and is still available as a type alias
with that name). A notable difference with the similar [is that it is a signed value instead of unsigned.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`core::time::Duration`Chrono currently only supports a small number of operations with [ core::time::Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html).
You can convert between both types with the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html#method.from_std)

`TimeDelta::from_std`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html#method.to_std)

`TimeDelta::to_std`[§](https://docs.rs#date-and-time)Date and Time

Chrono provides a [ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) type to represent a date and a time in a timezone.

For more abstract moment-in-time tracking such as internal timekeeping that is unconcerned with
timezones, consider [ std::time::SystemTime](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html), which tracks your system clock, or

[, which is an opaque but monotonically-increasing representation of a moment in time.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.Instant.html)

`std::time::Instant`[ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) is timezone-aware and must be constructed from a

[object, which defines how the local date is converted to and back from the UTC date. There are three well-known](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`[implementations:](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`-
`Utc`
-
`Local`
-
`FixedOffset``TimeZone`s into this type.

[ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)s with different

[types are distinct and do not mix, but can be converted to each other using the](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.with_timezone)

`DateTime::with_timezone`You can get the current date and time in the UTC time zone ([ Utc::now()](https://docs.rs/struct.Utc.html#method.now)) or in the local time
zone (

[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html#method.now)

`Local::now()````
use chrono::prelude::*;
let utc: DateTime<Utc> = Utc::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T12:45:59.324310806Z`
```
```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let local: DateTime<Local> = Local::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`
```
Alternatively, you can create your own date and time. This is a bit verbose due to Rust’s lack of function and method overloading, but in turn we get a rich combination of initialization methods.

```
use chrono::offset::MappedLocalTime;
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11).unwrap(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11Z`
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?
        .and_utc()
);
// July 8 is 188th day of the year 2014 (`o` for "ordinal")
assert_eq!(dt, NaiveDate::from_yo_opt(2014, 189)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc());
// July 8 is Tuesday in ISO week 28 of the year 2014.
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_isoywd_opt(2014, 28, Weekday::Tue)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc()
);
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
    .and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12)?
    .and_utc(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11.012Z`
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_micro_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000)?
        .and_utc()
);
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_nano_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000_000)?
        .and_utc()
);
// dynamic verification
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 21, 15, 33),
    MappedLocalTime::Single(
        NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?.and_hms_opt(21, 15, 33)?.and_utc()
    )
);
assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 80, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 38, 21, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
// other time zone objects can be used to construct a local datetime.
// obviously, `local_dt` is normally different from `dt`, but `fixed_dt` should be identical.
let local_dt = Local
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8).unwrap().and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12).unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
let fixed_dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
    .unwrap()
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)
            .unwrap()
            .and_hms_milli_opt(18, 10, 11, 12)
            .unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt, fixed_dt);
```
Various properties are available to the date and time, and can be altered individually. Most of
them are defined in the traits [ Datelike](https://docs.rs/trait.Datelike.html) and

[which you should](https://docs.rs/trait.Timelike.html)

`Timelike``use` before.
Addition and subtraction is also supported.
The following illustrates most supported operations to the date and time:```
use chrono::prelude::*;
use chrono::TimeDelta;
// assume this returned `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`:
let dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
    .unwrap()
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
            .unwrap()
            .and_hms_nano_opt(21, 45, 59, 324310806)
            .unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
// property accessors
assert_eq!((dt.year(), dt.month(), dt.day()), (2014, 11, 28));
assert_eq!((dt.month0(), dt.day0()), (10, 27)); // for unfortunate souls
assert_eq!((dt.hour(), dt.minute(), dt.second()), (21, 45, 59));
assert_eq!(dt.weekday(), Weekday::Fri);
assert_eq!(dt.weekday().number_from_monday(), 5); // Mon=1, ..., Sun=7
assert_eq!(dt.ordinal(), 332); // the day of year
assert_eq!(dt.num_days_from_ce(), 735565); // the number of days from and including Jan 1, 1
// time zone accessor and manipulation
assert_eq!(dt.offset().fix().local_minus_utc(), 9 * 3600);
assert_eq!(dt.timezone(), FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
assert_eq!(
    dt.with_timezone(&Utc),
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
        .unwrap()
        .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 45, 59, 324310806)
        .unwrap()
        .and_utc()
);
// a sample of property manipulations (validates dynamically)
assert_eq!(dt.with_day(29).unwrap().weekday(), Weekday::Sat); // 2014-11-29 is Saturday
assert_eq!(dt.with_day(32), None);
assert_eq!(dt.with_year(-300).unwrap().num_days_from_ce(), -109606); // November 29, 301 BCE
// arithmetic operations
let dt1 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 8, 9, 10).unwrap();
let dt2 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 10, 9, 8).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt1.signed_duration_since(dt2), TimeDelta::try_seconds(-2 * 3600 + 2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(dt2.signed_duration_since(dt1), TimeDelta::try_seconds(2 * 3600 - 2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
        + TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2001, 9, 9, 1, 46, 40).unwrap()
);
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
        - TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1938, 4, 24, 22, 13, 20).unwrap()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and Parsing

Formatting is done via the [ format](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.format) method, which format is equivalent to
the familiar

`strftime` format.See [ format::strftime](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and list of
specifiers.

The default `to_string` method and `{:?}` specifier also give a reasonable representation.
Chrono also provides [ to_rfc2822](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.to_rfc2822) and

[methods for well-known formats.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.to_rfc3339)

`to_rfc3339`Chrono now also provides date formatting in almost any language without the help of an
additional C library. This functionality is under the feature `unstable-locales`:

`chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["unstable-locales"] }`The `unstable-locales` feature requires and implies at least the `alloc` feature.

```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S").to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09");
assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), "Fri Nov 28 12:00:09 2014");
assert_eq!(
    dt.format_localized("%A %e %B %Y, %T", Locale::fr_BE).to_string(),
    "vendredi 28 novembre 2014, 12:00:09"
);
assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), dt.format("%c").to_string());
assert_eq!(dt.to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09 UTC");
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 28 Nov 2014 12:00:09 +0000");
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc3339(), "2014-11-28T12:00:09+00:00");
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt), "2014-11-28T12:00:09Z");
// Note that milli/nanoseconds are only printed if they are non-zero
let dt_nano = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 0, 9, 1)
    .unwrap()
    .and_utc();
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt_nano), "2014-11-28T12:00:09.000000001Z");
```
Parsing can be done with two methods:

-
The standard `FromStr``parse``DateTime<FixedOffset>`,`DateTime<Utc>`and`DateTime<Local>`values. This parses what the`{:?}`(`std::fmt::Debug`
-
`DateTime::parse_from_str``DateTime<FixedOffset>`. This should be used when the offset is a part of input and the caller cannot guess that. It*cannot*be used when the offset can be missing.`DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822``DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339`

More detailed control over the parsing process is available via [ format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html) module.

```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
let fixed_dt = dt.with_timezone(&FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
// method 1
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T12:00:09Z".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>(), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
// method 2
assert_eq!(
    DateTime::parse_from_str("2014-11-28 21:00:09 +09:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z"),
    Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
);
assert_eq!(
    DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 28 Nov 2014 21:00:09 +0900"),
    Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
);
assert_eq!(DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00"), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
// oops, the year is missing!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
// oops, the format string does not include the year at all!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T").is_err());
// oops, the weekday is incorrect!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Sat Nov 28 12:00:09 2014", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
```
Again: See [ format::strftime](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and
list of specifiers.

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-from-and-to-epoch-timestamps)Conversion from and to EPOCH timestamps

Use [ DateTime::from_timestamp(seconds, nanoseconds)](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.from_timestamp)
to construct a

[from a UNIX timestamp (seconds, nanoseconds that passed since January 1st 1970).](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime<Utc>`Use [ DateTime.timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.timestamp) to get the timestamp (in seconds)
from a

[. Additionally, you can use](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime`[to get the number of additional number of nanoseconds.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.timestamp_subsec_nanos)

`DateTime.timestamp_subsec_nanos````
// We need the trait in scope to use Utc::timestamp().
use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
// Construct a datetime from epoch:
let dt: DateTime<Utc> = DateTime::from_timestamp_secs(1_500_000_000).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000");
// Get epoch value from a datetime:
let dt = DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000").unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp(), 1_500_000_000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#naive-date-and-time)Naive date and time

Chrono provides naive counterparts to `Date`, (non-existent) `Time` and `DateTime` as
[ NaiveDate](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDate.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveTime.html)

`NaiveTime`[respectively.](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html)

`NaiveDateTime`They have almost equivalent interfaces as their timezone-aware twins, but are not associated to time zones obviously and can be quite low-level. They are mostly useful for building blocks for higher-level types.

Timezone-aware `DateTime` and `Date` types have two methods returning naive versions:
[ naive_local](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.naive_local) returns a view to the naive local time,
and

[returns a view to the naive UTC time.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.naive_utc)

`naive_utc`[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- Only the proleptic Gregorian calendar (i.e. extended to support older dates) is supported.
- Date types are limited to about +/- 262,000 years from the common epoch.
- Time types are limited to nanosecond accuracy.
- Leap seconds can be represented, but Chrono does not fully support them.
See [Leap Second Handling](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveTime.html#leap-second-handling).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-requirements)Rust version requirements

The Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) is currently **Rust 1.61.0**.

The MSRV is explicitly tested in CI. It may be bumped in minor releases, but this is not done lightly.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-between-chrono-and-time-01)Relation between chrono and time 0.1

Rust first had a `time` module added to `std` in its 0.7 release. It later moved to
`libextra`, and then to a `libtime` library shipped alongside the standard library. In 2014
work on chrono started in order to provide a full-featured date and time library in Rust.
Some improvements from chrono made it into the standard library; notably, `chrono::Duration`
was included as `std::time::Duration` ([rust#15934](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/15934)) in 2014.

In preparation of Rust 1.0 at the end of 2014 `libtime` was moved out of the Rust distro and
into the `time` crate to eventually be redesigned ([rust#18832](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18832#issuecomment-62448221), [rust#18858](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18858)), like the
`num` and `rand` crates. Of course chrono kept its dependency on this `time` crate. `time`
started re-exporting `std::time::Duration` during this period. Later, the standard library was
changed to have a more limited unsigned `Duration` type ([rust#24920](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/24920), [RFC 1040](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/1040-duration-reform.html)), while the
`time` crate kept the full functionality with `time::Duration`. `time::Duration` had been a
part of chrono’s public API.

By 2016 `time` 0.1 lived under the `rust-lang-deprecated` organisation and was not actively
maintained ([time#136](https://github.com/time-rs/time/issues/136)). chrono absorbed the platform functionality and `Duration` type of the
`time` crate in [chrono#478](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/478) (the work started in [chrono#286](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/286)). In order to preserve
compatibility with downstream crates depending on `time` and `chrono` sharing a `Duration`
type, chrono kept depending on time 0.1. chrono offered the option to opt out of the `time`
dependency by disabling the `oldtime` feature (swapping it out for an effectively similar
chrono type). In 2019, @jhpratt took over maintenance on the `time` crate and released what
amounts to a new crate as `time` 0.2.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-advisories)Security advisories

In November of 2020 [CVE-2020-26235](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-26235) and [RUSTSEC-2020-0071](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0071) were opened against the `time` crate.
@quininer had found that calls to `localtime_r` may be unsound ([chrono#499](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/499)). Eventually, almost
a year later, this was also made into a security advisory against chrono as [RUSTSEC-2020-0159](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0159.html),
which had platform code similar to `time`.

On Unix-like systems a process is given a timezone id or description via the `TZ` environment
variable. We need this timezone data to calculate the current local time from a value that is
in UTC, such as the time from the system clock. `time` 0.1 and chrono used the POSIX function
`localtime_r` to do the conversion to local time, which reads the `TZ` variable.

Rust assumes the environment to be writable and uses locks to access it from multiple threads.
Some other programming languages and libraries use similar locking strategies, but these are
typically not shared across languages. More importantly, POSIX declares modifying the
environment in a multi-threaded process as unsafe, and `getenv` in libc can’t be changed to
take a lock because it returns a pointer to the data (see [rust#27970](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27970) for more discussion).

Since version 4.20 chrono no longer uses `localtime_r`, instead using Rust code to query the
timezone (from the `TZ` variable or via `iana-time-zone` as a fallback) and work with data
from the system timezone database directly. The code for this was forked from the [tz-rs crate](https://crates.io/crates/tz-rs)
by @x-hgg-x. As such, chrono now respects the Rust lock when reading the `TZ` environment
variable. In general, code should avoid modifying the environment.

[§](https://docs.rs#removing-time-01)Removing time 0.1

Because time 0.1 has been unmaintained for years, however, the security advisory mentioned
above has not been addressed. While chrono maintainers were careful not to break backwards
compatibility with the `time::Duration` type, there has been a long stream of issues from
users inquiring about the time 0.1 dependency with the vulnerability. We investigated the
potential breakage of removing the time 0.1 dependency in [chrono#1095](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/1095) using a crater-like
experiment and determined that the potential for breaking (public) dependencies is very low.
We reached out to those few crates that did still depend on compatibility with time 0.1.

As such, for chrono 0.4.30 we have decided to swap out the time 0.1 `Duration` implementation
for a local one that will offer a strict superset of the existing API going forward. This
will prevent most downstream users from being affected by the security vulnerability in time
0.1 while minimizing the ecosystem impact of semver-incompatible version churn.

# chrono/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Chrono: Date and Time for Rust
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Chrono aims to provide all functionality needed to do correct operations on dates and times in
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! the [proleptic Gregorian calendar]:
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! * The [`DateTime`] type is timezone-aware by default, with separate timezone-naive types.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! * Operations that may produce an invalid or ambiguous date and time return `Option` or
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!   [`MappedLocalTime`].
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! * Configurable parsing and formatting with a `strftime` inspired date and time formatting
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   syntax.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! * The [`Local`] timezone works with the current timezone of the OS.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! * Types and operations are implemented to be reasonably efficient.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Timezone data is not shipped with chrono by default to limit binary sizes. Use the companion
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! crate [Chrono-TZ] or [`tzfile`] for full timezone support.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [proleptic Gregorian calendar]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proleptic_Gregorian_calendar
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! [Chrono-TZ]: https://crates.io/crates/chrono-tz
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! [`tzfile`]: https://crates.io/crates/tzfile
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ### Features
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! Chrono supports various runtime environments and operating systems, and has several features
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! that may be enabled or disabled.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! Default features:
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - `alloc`: Enable features that depend on allocation (primarily string formatting).
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! - `std`: Enables functionality that depends on the standard library. This is a superset of
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   `alloc` and adds interoperation with standard library types and traits.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! - `clock`: Enables reading the local timezone (`Local`). This is a superset of `now`.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! - `now`: Enables reading the system time (`now`).
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! - `wasmbind`: Interface with the JS Date API for the `wasm32` target.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! Optional features:
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! - `serde`: Enable serialization/deserialization via [serde].
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! - `rkyv`: Deprecated, use the `rkyv-*` features.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! - `rkyv-16`: Enable serialization/deserialization via [rkyv],
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!   using 16-bit integers for integral `*size` types.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! - `rkyv-32`: Enable serialization/deserialization via [rkyv],
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!   using 32-bit integers for integral `*size` types.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! - `rkyv-64`: Enable serialization/deserialization via [rkyv],
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!   using 64-bit integers for integral `*size` types.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! - `rkyv-validation`: Enable rkyv validation support using `bytecheck`.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! - `arbitrary`: Construct arbitrary instances of a type with the Arbitrary crate.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! - `unstable-locales`: Enable localization. This adds various methods with a `_localized` suffix.
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!   The implementation and API may change or even be removed in a patch release. Feedback welcome.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! - `oldtime`: This feature no longer has any effect; it used to offer compatibility with the
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!   `time` 0.1 crate.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! Note: The `rkyv{,-16,-32,-64}` features are mutually exclusive.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! See the [cargo docs] for examples of specifying features.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! [serde]: https://github.com/serde-rs/serde
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! [rkyv]: https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! [cargo docs]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#choosing-features
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! ## Overview
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ### Time delta / Duration
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! Chrono has a [`TimeDelta`] type to represent the magnitude of a time span. This is an "accurate"
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! duration represented as seconds and nanoseconds, and does not represent "nominal" components
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! such as days or months.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! The [`TimeDelta`] type was previously named `Duration` (and is still available as a type alias
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! with that name). A notable difference with the similar [`core::time::Duration`] is that it is a
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! signed value instead of unsigned.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! Chrono currently only supports a small number of operations with [`core::time::Duration`].
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! You can convert between both types with the [`TimeDelta::from_std`] and [`TimeDelta::to_std`]
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! methods.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! ### Date and Time
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! Chrono provides a [`DateTime`] type to represent a date and a time in a timezone.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! For more abstract moment-in-time tracking such as internal timekeeping that is unconcerned with
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! timezones, consider [`std::time::SystemTime`], which tracks your system clock, or
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! [`std::time::Instant`], which is an opaque but monotonically-increasing representation of a
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! moment in time.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! [`DateTime`] is timezone-aware and must be constructed from a [`TimeZone`] object, which defines
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! how the local date is converted to and back from the UTC date.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! There are three well-known [`TimeZone`] implementations:
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! * [`Utc`] specifies the UTC time zone. It is most efficient.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! * [`Local`] specifies the system local time zone.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! * [`FixedOffset`] specifies an arbitrary, fixed time zone such as UTC+09:00 or UTC-10:30.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!   This often results from the parsed textual date and time. Since it stores the most information
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!   and does not depend on the system environment, you would want to normalize other `TimeZone`s
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!   into this type.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! [`DateTime`]s with different [`TimeZone`] types are distinct and do not mix, but can be
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! converted to each other using the [`DateTime::with_timezone`] method.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! You can get the current date and time in the UTC time zone ([`Utc::now()`]) or in the local time
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! zone ([`Local::now()`]).
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! ```
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! # #[cfg(feature = "now")] {
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! let utc: DateTime<Utc> = Utc::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T12:45:59.324310806Z`
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! # let _ = utc;
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! # }
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! ```
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! ```
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! # #[cfg(feature = "clock")] {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! let local: DateTime<Local> = Local::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! # let _ = local;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! # }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! Alternatively, you can create your own date and time. This is a bit verbose due to Rust's lack
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! of function and method overloading, but in turn we get a rich combination of initialization
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! methods.
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! ```
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! use chrono::offset::MappedLocalTime;
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # fn doctest() -> Option<()> {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11).unwrap(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11Z`
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! assert_eq!(
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     dt,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!         .and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!         .and_utc()
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! );
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! // July 8 is 188th day of the year 2014 (`o` for "ordinal")
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! assert_eq!(dt, NaiveDate::from_yo_opt(2014, 189)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc());
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! // July 8 is Tuesday in ISO week 28 of the year 2014.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! assert_eq!(
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!     dt,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     NaiveDate::from_isoywd_opt(2014, 28, Weekday::Tue)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc()
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! );
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     .and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12)?
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     .and_utc(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11.012Z`
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! assert_eq!(
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     dt,
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!     NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!         .and_hms_micro_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000)?
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!         .and_utc()
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! );
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! assert_eq!(
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     dt,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!         .and_hms_nano_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000_000)?
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!         .and_utc()
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! );
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! // dynamic verification
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! assert_eq!(
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 21, 15, 33),
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!     MappedLocalTime::Single(
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!         NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?.and_hms_opt(21, 15, 33)?.and_utc()
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!     )
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! );
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 80, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 38, 21, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! # #[cfg(feature = "clock")] {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! // other time zone objects can be used to construct a local datetime.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! // obviously, `local_dt` is normally different from `dt`, but `fixed_dt` should be identical.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! let local_dt = Local
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!     .from_local_datetime(
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!         &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8).unwrap().and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12).unwrap(),
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!     )
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!     .unwrap();
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! let fixed_dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!     .unwrap()
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!     .from_local_datetime(
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!         &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!             .unwrap()
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!             .and_hms_milli_opt(18, 10, 11, 12)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!             .unwrap(),
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!     )
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!     .unwrap();
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! assert_eq!(dt, fixed_dt);
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! # let _ = local_dt;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! # }
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! # Some(())
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! # }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! # doctest().unwrap();
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! ```
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! Various properties are available to the date and time, and can be altered individually. Most of
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! them are defined in the traits [`Datelike`] and [`Timelike`] which you should `use` before.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! Addition and subtraction is also supported.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! The following illustrates most supported operations to the date and time:
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! ```rust
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! use chrono::TimeDelta;
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! // assume this returned `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`:
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! let dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!     .unwrap()
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!     .from_local_datetime(
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!         &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//!             .unwrap()
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!             .and_hms_nano_opt(21, 45, 59, 324310806)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!             .unwrap(),
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!     )
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!     .unwrap();
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! // property accessors
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! assert_eq!((dt.year(), dt.month(), dt.day()), (2014, 11, 28));
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! assert_eq!((dt.month0(), dt.day0()), (10, 27)); // for unfortunate souls
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! assert_eq!((dt.hour(), dt.minute(), dt.second()), (21, 45, 59));
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! assert_eq!(dt.weekday(), Weekday::Fri);
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! assert_eq!(dt.weekday().number_from_monday(), 5); // Mon=1, ..., Sun=7
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! assert_eq!(dt.ordinal(), 332); // the day of year
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! assert_eq!(dt.num_days_from_ce(), 735565); // the number of days from and including Jan 1, 1
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! // time zone accessor and manipulation
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! assert_eq!(dt.offset().fix().local_minus_utc(), 9 * 3600);
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! assert_eq!(dt.timezone(), FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! assert_eq!(
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!     dt.with_timezone(&Utc),
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!     NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!         .unwrap()
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!         .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 45, 59, 324310806)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!         .unwrap()
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!         .and_utc()
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! );
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! // a sample of property manipulations (validates dynamically)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! assert_eq!(dt.with_day(29).unwrap().weekday(), Weekday::Sat); // 2014-11-29 is Saturday
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! assert_eq!(dt.with_day(32), None);
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! assert_eq!(dt.with_year(-300).unwrap().num_days_from_ce(), -109606); // November 29, 301 BCE
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! // arithmetic operations
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! let dt1 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 8, 9, 10).unwrap();
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! let dt2 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 10, 9, 8).unwrap();
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! assert_eq!(dt1.signed_duration_since(dt2), TimeDelta::try_seconds(-2 * 3600 + 2).unwrap());
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! assert_eq!(dt2.signed_duration_since(dt1), TimeDelta::try_seconds(2 * 3600 - 2).unwrap());
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! assert_eq!(
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!     Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!         + TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!     Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2001, 9, 9, 1, 46, 40).unwrap()
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! );
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! assert_eq!(
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!     Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!         - TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!     Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1938, 4, 24, 22, 13, 20).unwrap()
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! );
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! ```
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! ### Formatting and Parsing
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! Formatting is done via the [`format`](DateTime::format()) method, which format is equivalent to
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! the familiar `strftime` format.
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! See [`format::strftime`](format::strftime#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and list of
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! specifiers.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! The default `to_string` method and `{:?}` specifier also give a reasonable representation.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! Chrono also provides [`to_rfc2822`](DateTime::to_rfc2822) and
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! [`to_rfc3339`](DateTime::to_rfc3339) methods for well-known formats.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! Chrono now also provides date formatting in almost any language without the help of an
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! additional C library. This functionality is under the feature `unstable-locales`:
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! ```toml
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["unstable-locales"] }
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! ```
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! The `unstable-locales` feature requires and implies at least the `alloc` feature.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! ```rust
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! # #[allow(unused_imports)]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "unstable-locales", feature = "alloc"))]
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! # fn test() {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! assert_eq!(dt.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S").to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09");
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), "Fri Nov 28 12:00:09 2014");
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! assert_eq!(
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!     dt.format_localized("%A %e %B %Y, %T", Locale::fr_BE).to_string(),
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!     "vendredi 28 novembre 2014, 12:00:09"
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! );
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), dt.format("%c").to_string());
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! assert_eq!(dt.to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09 UTC");
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 28 Nov 2014 12:00:09 +0000");
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc3339(), "2014-11-28T12:00:09+00:00");
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt), "2014-11-28T12:00:09Z");
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! // Note that milli/nanoseconds are only printed if they are non-zero
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! let dt_nano = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!     .unwrap()
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!     .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 0, 9, 1)
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!     .unwrap()
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!     .and_utc();
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt_nano), "2014-11-28T12:00:09.000000001Z");
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! # }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! # #[cfg(not(all(feature = "unstable-locales", feature = "alloc")))]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! # fn test() {}
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! # if cfg!(all(feature = "unstable-locales", feature = "alloc")) {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! #    test();
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! # }
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! ```
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! Parsing can be done with two methods:
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! 1. The standard [`FromStr`](std::str::FromStr) trait (and [`parse`](str::parse) method on a
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!    string) can be used for parsing `DateTime<FixedOffset>`, `DateTime<Utc>` and
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!    `DateTime<Local>` values. This parses what the `{:?}` ([`std::fmt::Debug`] format specifier
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!    prints, and requires the offset to be present.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! 2. [`DateTime::parse_from_str`] parses a date and time with offsets and returns
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!    `DateTime<FixedOffset>`. This should be used when the offset is a part of input and the
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!    caller cannot guess that. It *cannot* be used when the offset can be missing.
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!    [`DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822`] and [`DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339`] are similar but for
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!    well-known formats.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! More detailed control over the parsing process is available via [`format`](mod@format) module.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! ```rust
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! use chrono::prelude::*;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! let fixed_dt = dt.with_timezone(&FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! // method 1
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! assert_eq!("2014-11-28T12:00:09Z".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>(), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! // method 2
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! assert_eq!(
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!     DateTime::parse_from_str("2014-11-28 21:00:09 +09:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z"),
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!     Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! );
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! assert_eq!(
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!     DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 28 Nov 2014 21:00:09 +0900"),
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!     Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//! );
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! assert_eq!(DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00"), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! // oops, the year is missing!
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! // oops, the format string does not include the year at all!
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T").is_err());
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//! // oops, the weekday is incorrect!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Sat Nov 28 12:00:09 2014", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//! ```
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//! Again: See [`format::strftime`](format::strftime#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! list of specifiers.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//! ### Conversion from and to EPOCH timestamps
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! Use [`DateTime::from_timestamp(seconds, nanoseconds)`](DateTime::from_timestamp)
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! to construct a [`DateTime<Utc>`] from a UNIX timestamp
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//! (seconds, nanoseconds that passed since January 1st 1970).
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//!
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//! Use [`DateTime.timestamp`](DateTime::timestamp) to get the timestamp (in seconds)
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//! from a [`DateTime`]. Additionally, you can use
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! [`DateTime.timestamp_subsec_nanos`](DateTime::timestamp_subsec_nanos)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//! to get the number of additional number of nanoseconds.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//!
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//! ```
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//! # #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//! // We need the trait in scope to use Utc::timestamp().
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//! use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//!
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//! // Construct a datetime from epoch:
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//! let dt: DateTime<Utc> = DateTime::from_timestamp_secs(1_500_000_000).unwrap();
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000");
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//!
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//! // Get epoch value from a datetime:
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! let dt = DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000").unwrap();
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//! assert_eq!(dt.timestamp(), 1_500_000_000);
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//! # }
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! ```
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! ### Naive date and time
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//!
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//! Chrono provides naive counterparts to `Date`, (non-existent) `Time` and `DateTime` as
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//! [`NaiveDate`], [`NaiveTime`] and [`NaiveDateTime`] respectively.
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! They have almost equivalent interfaces as their timezone-aware twins, but are not associated to
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! time zones obviously and can be quite low-level. They are mostly useful for building blocks for
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//! higher-level types.
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//!
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//! Timezone-aware `DateTime` and `Date` types have two methods returning naive versions:
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//! [`naive_local`](DateTime::naive_local) returns a view to the naive local time,
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! and [`naive_utc`](DateTime::naive_utc) returns a view to the naive UTC time.
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//!
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! ## Limitations
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//!
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! * Only the proleptic Gregorian calendar (i.e. extended to support older dates) is supported.
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! * Date types are limited to about +/- 262,000 years from the common epoch.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! * Time types are limited to nanosecond accuracy.
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! * Leap seconds can be represented, but Chrono does not fully support them.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//!   See [Leap Second Handling](NaiveTime#leap-second-handling).
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//!
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! ## Rust version requirements
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//!
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//! The Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) is currently **Rust 1.61.0**.
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//!
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! The MSRV is explicitly tested in CI. It may be bumped in minor releases, but this is not done
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//! lightly.
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//! ## Relation between chrono and time 0.1
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//!
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//! Rust first had a `time` module added to `std` in its 0.7 release. It later moved to
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! `libextra`, and then to a `libtime` library shipped alongside the standard library. In 2014
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//! work on chrono started in order to provide a full-featured date and time library in Rust.
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//! Some improvements from chrono made it into the standard library; notably, `chrono::Duration`
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//! was included as `std::time::Duration` ([rust#15934]) in 2014.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//!
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//! In preparation of Rust 1.0 at the end of 2014 `libtime` was moved out of the Rust distro and
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//! into the `time` crate to eventually be redesigned ([rust#18832], [rust#18858]), like the
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//! `num` and `rand` crates. Of course chrono kept its dependency on this `time` crate. `time`
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//! started re-exporting `std::time::Duration` during this period. Later, the standard library was
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//! changed to have a more limited unsigned `Duration` type ([rust#24920], [RFC 1040]), while the
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//! `time` crate kept the full functionality with `time::Duration`. `time::Duration` had been a
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//! part of chrono's public API.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//!
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//! By 2016 `time` 0.1 lived under the `rust-lang-deprecated` organisation and was not actively
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//! maintained ([time#136]). chrono absorbed the platform functionality and `Duration` type of the
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//! `time` crate in [chrono#478] (the work started in [chrono#286]). In order to preserve
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//! compatibility with downstream crates depending on `time` and `chrono` sharing a `Duration`
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//! type, chrono kept depending on time 0.1. chrono offered the option to opt out of the `time`
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//! dependency by disabling the `oldtime` feature (swapping it out for an effectively similar
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//! chrono type). In 2019, @jhpratt took over maintenance on the `time` crate and released what
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//! amounts to a new crate as `time` 0.2.
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//!
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//! [rust#15934]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/15934
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! [rust#18832]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18832#issuecomment-62448221
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//! [rust#18858]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18858
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//! [rust#24920]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/24920
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! [RFC 1040]: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/1040-duration-reform.html
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//! [time#136]: https://github.com/time-rs/time/issues/136
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//! [chrono#286]: https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/286
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! [chrono#478]: https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/478
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//!
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! ## Security advisories
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//!
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! In November of 2020 [CVE-2020-26235] and [RUSTSEC-2020-0071] were opened against the `time` crate.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//! @quininer had found that calls to `localtime_r` may be unsound ([chrono#499]). Eventually, almost
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! a year later, this was also made into a security advisory against chrono as [RUSTSEC-2020-0159],
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//! which had platform code similar to `time`.
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//!
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! On Unix-like systems a process is given a timezone id or description via the `TZ` environment
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//! variable. We need this timezone data to calculate the current local time from a value that is
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//! in UTC, such as the time from the system clock. `time` 0.1 and chrono used the POSIX function
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//! `localtime_r` to do the conversion to local time, which reads the `TZ` variable.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//!
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//! Rust assumes the environment to be writable and uses locks to access it from multiple threads.
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//! Some other programming languages and libraries use similar locking strategies, but these are
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//! typically not shared across languages. More importantly, POSIX declares modifying the
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//! environment in a multi-threaded process as unsafe, and `getenv` in libc can't be changed to
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//! take a lock because it returns a pointer to the data (see [rust#27970] for more discussion).
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//! Since version 4.20 chrono no longer uses `localtime_r`, instead using Rust code to query the
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//! timezone (from the `TZ` variable or via `iana-time-zone` as a fallback) and work with data
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//! from the system timezone database directly. The code for this was forked from the [tz-rs crate]
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//! by @x-hgg-x. As such, chrono now respects the Rust lock when reading the `TZ` environment
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//! variable. In general, code should avoid modifying the environment.
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//!
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//! [CVE-2020-26235]: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-26235
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//! [RUSTSEC-2020-0071]: https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0071
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//! [chrono#499]: https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/499
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//! [RUSTSEC-2020-0159]: https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0159.html
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//! [rust#27970]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27970
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//! [chrono#677]: https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/677
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//! [tz-rs crate]: https://crates.io/crates/tz-rs
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//!
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//! ## Removing time 0.1
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//!
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! Because time 0.1 has been unmaintained for years, however, the security advisory mentioned
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//! above has not been addressed. While chrono maintainers were careful not to break backwards
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! compatibility with the `time::Duration` type, there has been a long stream of issues from
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//! users inquiring about the time 0.1 dependency with the vulnerability. We investigated the
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//! potential breakage of removing the time 0.1 dependency in [chrono#1095] using a crater-like
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//! experiment and determined that the potential for breaking (public) dependencies is very low.
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//! We reached out to those few crates that did still depend on compatibility with time 0.1.
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//!
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! As such, for chrono 0.4.30 we have decided to swap out the time 0.1 `Duration` implementation
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//! for a local one that will offer a strict superset of the existing API going forward. This
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! will prevent most downstream users from being affected by the security vulnerability in time
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//! 0.1 while minimizing the ecosystem impact of semver-incompatible version churn.
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//!
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//! [chrono#1095]: https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/1095
[502](https://docs.rs#502)

[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// Serialization/Deserialization with serde
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// The [`DateTime`] type has default implementations for (de)serializing to/from the [RFC 3339]
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// format. This module provides alternatives for serializing to timestamps.
[600](https://docs.rs#600)///
[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// The alternatives are for use with serde's [`with` annotation] combined with the module name.
[602](https://docs.rs#602)/// Alternatively the individual `serialize` and `deserialize` functions in each module can be used
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// with serde's [`serialize_with`] and [`deserialize_with`] annotations.
[604](https://docs.rs#604)///
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// *Available on crate feature 'serde' only.*
[606](https://docs.rs#606)///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)/// [RFC 3339]: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3339
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// [`with` annotation]: https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// [`serialize_with`]: https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#serialize_with
[610](https://docs.rs#610)/// [`deserialize_with`]: https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#deserialize_with
[611](https://docs.rs#611)#[cfg(feature = "serde")]

[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// Create a custom `de::Error` with `SerdeError::InvalidTimestamp`.
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    pub(crate) fn invalid_ts<E, T>(value: T) -> E
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    where
[621](https://docs.rs#621)        E: de::Error,
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        T: fmt::Display,
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    {
[624](https://docs.rs#624)        E::custom(SerdeError::InvalidTimestamp(value))
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    }
[626](https://docs.rs#626)
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    enum SerdeError<T: fmt::Display> {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)        InvalidTimestamp(T),
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    }
[630](https://docs.rs#630)
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    impl<T: fmt::Display> fmt::Display for SerdeError<T> {

[633](https://docs.rs#633)            match self {
[634](https://docs.rs#634)                SerdeError::InvalidTimestamp(ts) => {
[635](https://docs.rs#635)                    write!(f, "value is not a legal timestamp: {ts}")
[636](https://docs.rs#636)                }
[637](https://docs.rs#637)            }
[638](https://docs.rs#638)        }
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    }

# DateTime in chrono - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/chrono/0.4.45/chrono/struct.DateTime.html

`pub struct DateTime<Tz: `[TimeZone](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

ISO 8601 combined date and time with time zone.

There are some constructors implemented here (the `from_*` methods), but
the general-purpose constructors are all via the methods on the
[ TimeZone](https://docs.rs/offset/trait.TimeZone.html) implementations.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

    datetime: [NaiveDateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html),
    offset: Tz::[Offset](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html#associatedtype.Offset),
) -> [DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<Tz>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#94-99)

#### pub const fn [from_naive_utc_and_offset](https://docs.rs#method.from_naive_utc_and_offset)(
    datetime: [NaiveDateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html),
    offset: Tz::[Offset](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html#associatedtype.Offset),
) -> [DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<Tz>

Makes a new `DateTime` from its components: a `NaiveDateTime` in UTC and an `Offset`.

This is a low-level method, intended for use cases such as deserializing a `DateTime` or
passing it through FFI.

For regular use you will probably want to use a method such as
[ TimeZone::from_local_datetime](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html#method.from_local_datetime) or

[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html#method.and_local_timezone)

`NaiveDateTime::and_local_timezone`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use chrono::{DateTime, Local};
let dt = Local::now();
// Get components
let naive_utc = dt.naive_utc();
let offset = dt.offset().clone();
// Serialize, pass through FFI... and recreate the `DateTime`:
let dt_new = DateTime::<Local>::from_naive_utc_and_offset(naive_utc, offset);
assert_eq!(dt, dt_new);
```

Makes a new `DateTime` from a `NaiveDateTime` in *local* time and an `Offset`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the local datetime can’t be converted to UTC because it would be out of range.

This can happen if `datetime` is near the end of the representable range of `NaiveDateTime`,
and the offset from UTC pushes it beyond that.

Retrieves the date component with an associated timezone.

Unless you are immediately planning on turning this into a `DateTime`
with the same timezone you should use the [ date_naive](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.date_naive) method.

[ NaiveDate](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDate.html) is a more well-defined type, and has more traits implemented on it,
so should be preferred to

[any time you truly want to operate on dates.](https://docs.rs/struct.Date.html)

[. This method will panic if the offset from UTC would push the local date outside of the representable range of a](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html)

`NaiveDateTime`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Date.html)

`NaiveDate`[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let date: DateTime<Utc> = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();

    FixedOffset::east_opt(23).unwrap().with_ymd_and_hms(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();

```
Returns the number of non-leap seconds since January 1, 1970 0:00:00 UTC (aka “UNIX timestamp”).

The reverse operation of creating a [ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) from a timestamp can be performed
using

[or](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.from_timestamp)

`from_timestamp`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html#method.timestamp_opt)

`TimeZone::timestamp_opt````
use chrono::{DateTime, TimeZone, Utc};
let dt: DateTime<Utc> = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2015, 5, 15, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp(), 1431648000);
assert_eq!(DateTime::from_timestamp(dt.timestamp(), dt.timestamp_subsec_nanos()).unwrap(), dt);
```

#### pub const fn [timestamp_millis](https://docs.rs#method.timestamp_millis)(&self) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)

Returns the number of non-leap-milliseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use chrono::{NaiveDate, Utc};
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(1970, 1, 1)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_milli_opt(0, 0, 1, 444)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_millis(), 1_444);
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2001, 9, 9)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_milli_opt(1, 46, 40, 555)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_millis(), 1_000_000_000_555);
```

#### pub const fn [timestamp_nanos](https://docs.rs#method.timestamp_nanos)(&self) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)

use `timestamp_nanos_opt()` instead

Returns the number of non-leap-nanoseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

An `i64` with nanosecond precision can span a range of ~584 years. This function panics on
an out of range `DateTime`.

The dates that can be represented as nanoseconds are between 1677-09-21T00:12:43.145224192 and 2262-04-11T23:47:16.854775807.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#350-364)#### pub const fn [timestamp_nanos_opt](https://docs.rs#method.timestamp_nanos_opt)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#350-364)

#### pub const fn [timestamp_nanos_opt](https://docs.rs#method.timestamp_nanos_opt)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html)>

Returns the number of non-leap-nanoseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

An `i64` with nanosecond precision can span a range of ~584 years. This function returns
`None` on an out of range `DateTime`.

The dates that can be represented as nanoseconds are between 1677-09-21T00:12:43.145224192 and 2262-04-11T23:47:16.854775807.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use chrono::{NaiveDate, Utc};
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(1970, 1, 1)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(0, 0, 1, 444)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), Some(1_000_000_444));
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2001, 9, 9)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(1, 46, 40, 555)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), Some(1_000_000_000_000_000_555));
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(1677, 9, 21)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(0, 12, 43, 145_224_192)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), Some(-9_223_372_036_854_775_808));
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2262, 4, 11)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(23, 47, 16, 854_775_807)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), Some(9_223_372_036_854_775_807));
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(1677, 9, 21)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(0, 12, 43, 145_224_191)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), None);
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2262, 4, 11)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(23, 47, 16, 854_775_808)
    .unwrap()
    .and_local_timezone(Utc)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp_nanos_opt(), None);
```

This is a convenience wrapper around [ DateTime::from_timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.from_timestamp),

[to avoid a closure.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.map)

`TimeZone::timestamp_opt`[; if you need to create a](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.with_timezone)

`DateTime::from_timestamp_nanos`[§](https://docs.rs#errors-9)Errors

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

Using [ Option::and_then](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.and_then):

```
Using [ Iterator::map](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.map):

let v = vec![i64::MIN, 1_000_000_000, 1_234_567_890, i64::MAX];

    .into_iter()

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1051-1056)#### pub fn [parse_from_rfc2822](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_rfc2822)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1051-1056)

#### pub fn [parse_from_rfc2822](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_rfc2822)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

Parses an RFC 2822 date-and-time string into a `DateTime<FixedOffset>` value.

This parses valid RFC 2822 datetime strings (such as `Tue, 1 Jul 2003 10:52:37 +0200`)
and returns a new [ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) instance with the parsed timezone as the

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)

`FixedOffset`RFC 2822 is the internet message standard that specifies the representation of times in HTTP and email headers. It is the 2001 revision of RFC 822, and is itself revised as RFC 5322 in 2008.

[§](https://docs.rs#support-for-the-obsolete-date-format)Support for the obsolete date format

- A 2-digit year is interpreted to be a year in 1950-2049.
- The standard allows comments and whitespace between many of the tokens. See [4.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822#section-4.3)and[Appendix A.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2822#appendix-A.5)
- Single letter ‘military’ time zone names are parsed as a `-0000`offset. They were defined with the wrong sign in RFC 822 and corrected in RFC 2822. But because the meaning is now ambiguous, the standard says they should be considered as`-0000`unless there is out-of-band information confirming their meaning. The exception is`Z`, which remains identical to`+0000`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
assert_eq!(
    DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Wed, 18 Feb 2015 23:16:09 GMT").unwrap(),
    FixedOffset::east_opt(0).unwrap().with_ymd_and_hms(2015, 2, 18, 23, 16, 9).unwrap()
);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1071-1073)#### pub fn [parse_from_rfc3339](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_rfc3339)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1071-1073)

#### pub fn [parse_from_rfc3339](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_rfc3339)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

Parses an RFC 3339 date-and-time string into a `DateTime<FixedOffset>` value.

Parses all valid RFC 3339 values (as well as the subset of valid ISO 8601 values that are
also valid RFC 3339 date-and-time values) and returns a new [ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) with a

[corresponding to the parsed timezone. While RFC 3339 values come in a wide variety of shapes and sizes,](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)

`FixedOffset``1996-12-19T16:39:57-08:00` is an example of the most commonly
encountered variety of RFC 3339 formats.Why isn’t this named `parse_from_iso8601`? That’s because ISO 8601 allows representing
values in a wide range of formats, only some of which represent actual date-and-time
instances (rather than periods, ranges, dates, or times). Some valid ISO 8601 values are
also simultaneously valid RFC 3339 values, but not all RFC 3339 values are valid ISO 8601
values (or the other way around).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1104-1108)#### pub fn [parse_from_str](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_str)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), fmt: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1104-1108)

#### pub fn [parse_from_str](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_str)(s: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), fmt: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<[DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>>

Parses a string from a user-specified format into a `DateTime<FixedOffset>` value.

Note that this method *requires a timezone* in the input string. See
[ NaiveDateTime::parse_from_str](https://docs.rs/naive/struct.NaiveDateTime.html#method.parse_from_str)
for a version that does not require a timezone in the to-be-parsed str. The returned

[value will have a](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime`[reflecting the parsed timezone.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)

`FixedOffset`See the [ format::strftime module](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html) for supported format
sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
use chrono::{DateTime, FixedOffset, NaiveDate, TimeZone};
let dt = DateTime::parse_from_str("1983 Apr 13 12:09:14.274 +0000", "%Y %b %d %H:%M:%S%.3f %z");
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    Ok(FixedOffset::east_opt(0)
        .unwrap()
        .from_local_datetime(
            &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(1983, 4, 13)
                .unwrap()
                .and_hms_milli_opt(12, 9, 14, 274)
                .unwrap()
        )
        .unwrap())
);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1138-1145)#### pub fn [parse_and_remainder](https://docs.rs#method.parse_and_remainder)<'a>(
    s: &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    fmt: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<([DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>, &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/chrono/datetime/mod.rs.html#1138-1145)

#### pub fn [parse_and_remainder](https://docs.rs#method.parse_and_remainder)<'a>(
    s: &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    fmt: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
) -> [ParseResult](https://docs.rs/format/type.ParseResult.html)<([DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)<[FixedOffset](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)>, &'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))>

Parses a string from a user-specified format into a `DateTime<FixedOffset>` value, and a
slice with the remaining portion of the string.

Note that this method *requires a timezone* in the input string. See
[ NaiveDateTime::parse_and_remainder](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html#method.parse_and_remainder) for a version that does not
require a timezone in

`s`. The returned [value will have a](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime`[reflecting the parsed timezone.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedOffset.html)

`FixedOffset`See the [ format::strftime module](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html) for supported format
sequences.

Similar to [ parse_from_str](https://docs.rs#method.parse_from_str).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-12)Example

```
let (datetime, remainder) = DateTime::parse_and_remainder(
    "2015-02-18 23:16:09 +0200 trailing text",
    "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z",
)
.unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    datetime,
    FixedOffset::east_opt(2 * 3600).unwrap().with_ymd_and_hms(2015, 2, 18, 23, 16, 9).unwrap()
);
assert_eq!(remainder, " trailing text");
```

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-18)Panics

Panics if:

- The resulting date would be out of range.
- The local time at the resulting date does not exist or is ambiguous, for example during a daylight saving time transition.

Strongly consider using `DateTime<Tz>::checked_add_days` to get an `Option` instead.

As a part of Chrono’s [leap second handling], the addition assumes that **there is no leap
second ever**, except when the `NaiveDateTime` itself represents a leap second in which case
the assumption becomes that **there is exactly a single leap second ever**.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-7)Panics

Panics if the resulting date would be out of range.
Consider using [ DateTime<Tz>::checked_add_signed](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.checked_add_signed) to get an

`Option` instead.The result will be clamped to valid days in the resulting month, see `checked_add_months` for
details.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-13)Errors

Returns `None` if:

- The resulting date does not exist (February 29 in a non-leap year).
- The local time at the resulting date does not exist or is ambiguous, for example during a daylight saving time transition.
- The resulting UTC datetime would be out of range.
- The resulting local datetime would be out of range (unless the year remains the same).

Makes a new `DateTime` with the month number (starting from 1) changed.

Don’t combine multiple `Datelike::with_*` methods. The intermediate value may not exist.

See also the [ NaiveDate::with_month](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDate.html#method.with_month) method.

- The value for `month`is invalid.
- The local time at the resulting date does not exist or is ambiguous, for example during a daylight saving time transition.

Makes a new `DateTime` with the month number (starting from 0) changed.

See also the [ NaiveDate::with_month0](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDate.html#method.with_month0) method.

All of these examples are equivalent:

```
"2012-12-12T12:12:12Z".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>()?;
"2012-12-12 12:12:12Z".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>()?;
"2012-  12-12T12:  12:12Z".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>()?;
```
